hints: Expand the curve equation as $x^2y-6xy^2=9a^3$ and differentiate implicitly.
For a horizontal tangent set $dy/dx=0$ in the differentiated equation.
Factor the remaining condition in $x,y$; reject $y=0$ because $a\ne0$ makes it incompatible with the original curve.
Use the surviving relation between $x$ and $y$ in the original equation.
Solve consistently for the single point in terms of $a$, explaining why no other case remains.
walkthrough:
Differentiate both sides implicitly with respect to $x$ using the product rule:
$$\left(2xy + x^2\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right) - 6\left(y^2 + 2xy\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\right) = 0$$

Expand and collect terms with $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$:
$$2xy - 6y^2 + (x^2 - 12xy)\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{6y^2 - 2xy}{x^2 - 12xy} = \dfrac{2y(3y - x)}{x(x - 12y)}$$

A tangent parallel to the $x$-axis has $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$, so set the numerator to zero:
$$2y(3y - x) = 0 \implies y = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 3y$$
Test $y = 0$: substituting $y = 0$ into the curve equation gives $0 = 9a^3$, which is impossible since $a$ is a non-zero constant. Thus $y \neq 0$.

Substitute $x = 3y$ into the curve equation $xy(x - 6y) = 9a^3$:
$$(3y)(y)(3y - 6y) = 9a^3$$
$$3y^2(-3y) = 9a^3$$
$$-9y^3 = 9a^3 \implies y^3 = -a^3 \implies y = -a$$

Because $y^3 = -a^3$ has only one real root, there is only one point on the curve with a horizontal tangent, with coordinates:
$$(-3a, -a)$$
